# Locality Guide: Schenectady County, New York (1770–1850)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** 1809 from Albany County
- **County seat:** Schenectady City
- **Parent jurisdiction:** New York State (Albany County before 1809)
- **Population during period:** growing agricultural/merchant community; Niskayuna township was a rural Dutch Reformed farming community
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly Dutch-descended families in the Niskayuna/Glenville area; English, Scots-Irish and German settlers also present
- **Religious denominations:** Reformed Protestant Dutch Church (dominant in Niskayuna); Presbyterian, Episcopal, Methodist also present
- **Key historical events:** Revolutionary War disrupted record-keeping; county formation 1809 split Albany County records

## Boundary changes
- Before 1776: Schenectady area was part of Albany County, New York Colony
- 1776–1809: Schenectady was a town within Albany County, New York State
- 1809: Schenectady County formed from Albany County — records split at this date
- **Research implication:** Events before 1809 (including JPW's 1775 birth) were recorded under Albany County authority

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** 1880 (statewide mandatory registration)
- **Pre-1880:** Church records are the sole vital-event source for 1770–1850
- **Gaps:** No civil births, deaths, or marriages exist for the 1770–1850 period

### Church records
- **Primary denomination:** Reformed Protestant Dutch Church / Niskayuna Reformed Church
- **Record types:** Baptisms (doopregisters), marriages, burials, member rolls
- **FamilySearch collections:** 'New York, Births and Christenings, 1640-1962' (col. 1680842, 794,555 records); 'New York, Church Records, 1660-1954' (col. 2787817, 127,105 records); 'New York, Church and Civil Births and Baptisms, 1704-1962' (col. 2443988)
- **Niskayuna Reformed Dutch Church volumes:** At least one volume (IGN 007767898_015) covers marriages 1836–1861 (48% indexed, full-text searchable); baptism registers for the family period (1799–1817) are in FamilySearch collections — confirmed by the existing child christening records in tree.gedcomx.json
- **Language:** English by late 18th century; earlier records may be in Dutch

### Census records
- **Federal:** 1790, 1800, 1810, 1820, 1830, 1840, 1850 — all available; indexed on FamilySearch and Ancestry
- **New York State:** 1825, 1835, 1845 state censuses exist but coverage varies; 1845 is the most complete for Schenectady County
- **Access:** Federal censuses are indexed; state censuses may be browse-only for some years

### Probate and court records
- **Pre-1809:** Albany County Surrogate's Court (records in Albany County)
- **Post-1809:** Schenectady County Surrogate's Court
- **FamilySearch:** 'New York, Probate Records, 1629-1971' (col. 1920234) — browse-only images, 14M+ images; may contain wills and administrations naming death date and heirs
- **Access:** Browse-only — no name index; must locate the volume for Schenectady County and the relevant time period

### Land records
- **FamilySearch:** 'New York, Land Records, 1630-1975' (col. 2078654) — 65.5M records, indexed
- **Content:** Deeds, mortgages, patents; may name grantors/grantees and occasionally reference death

### Cemetery records
- **Niskayuna Reformed Church Cemetery:** Primary burial ground for the Witbeck family (confirmed by tree facts for Sarah Cragier, Anne Witbeck, Thomas Witbeck, Emmettie Witbeck)
- **FamilySearch:** 'New York, Cemetery Abstracts, 1800-1965' (col. 2552111, 175,959 records, 5,282 images)
- **Online:** FindAGrave and BillionGraves likely have entries for this well-documented cemetery

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Revolutionary War (JPW born 1775; father Gerrit L. served?); War of 1812
- **Record types:** Pension files (NARA), bounty land warrants, state militia rolls
- **Access:** NARA pension files are digitized on Fold3/Ancestry; FamilySearch has some compiled indexes

### Newspapers
- **Local papers:** Schenectady Cabinet (founded 1806); Albany Gazette/Albany Argus (cover Schenectady events pre-1809)
- **Online:** Chronicling America (Library of Congress), NYS Historic Newspapers — coverage varies; obituaries and legal notices may appear

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Key collections | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Births/Christenings 1640–1962; Church Records 1660–1954; Deaths & Burials 1795–1952; Cemetery Abstracts 1800–1965; Probate Records 1629–1971 (browse-only); Land Records 1630–1975 | Free |
| Ancestry | Federal censuses; New York state censuses; church record compilations; newspapers | Subscription |
| FindAGrave | Niskayuna Reformed Church Cemetery inscriptions | Free |

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| Schenectady County Surrogate's Court | Probate records 1809–present | In-person/mail |
| Albany County Surrogate's Court | Probate records pre-1809 | In-person/mail |
| Schenectady County Historical Society | Local church records, newspapers, family histories | In-person |
| New York State Archives, Albany | Colonial and early state records | In-person/online request |

## Records NOT online
- Schenectady County tax records for most of 1770–1850
- Some local church registers not microfilmed by FamilySearch
- Town-level vital record books (birth/death notices kept informally)

## Known record losses
- No major courthouse fires documented for Schenectady County; Albany County records largely intact
- Some early church registers deteriorated before microfilming

## Research tips
- **Always search both Albany County and Schenectady County** for events spanning the 1809 boundary year
- Search spelling variants: Witbeck, Witbeek, Witbeeck, Wittbeck, Witbek — Dutch Reformed registers often used Dutch spellings
- The Niskayuna Reformed Church baptism register (confirming children 1799–1817) is the best finding aid to locate JPW in church records — search the same volume for burial and death entries
- Probate records (browse-only) are a critical substitute for missing death certificates — search Schenectady County surrogate's index for John Perry Witbeck or his heirs
- New York state censuses (1825, 1835, 1845) can bracket a death date — if JPW appears in 1835 but not 1845, death was between those years
- Cemetery abstracting societies (DAR, local genealogical societies) often published Schenectady County cemetery inscriptions; check the Schenectady County Historical Society library

## Death Date of John Perry Witbeck — Proof Summary

### Research Question

What is the death date of John Perry Witbeck (born 10 March 1775, Niskayuna, Schenectady County, New York), as evidenced by church, civil, or probate records?

### Evidence

**Documented presence — lower bound (January 1803)**

A church baptism record in "New York, Church Records, 1660-1954" (FamilySearch, https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:2:QR6N-CF8K : accessed 2026-07-25) records the christening of Gertrude Witbeck on 10 January 1803 and names *John Perry Witbeck* as father and *Sarah Krigier* as mother.¹ This derivative source carries primary information reported by the parents at the time of the event. It establishes directly that John Perry Witbeck was alive as of 10 January 1803 — the latest record in which he is documented as present. The mother’s surname “Krigier” is a recognized phonetic variant of “Cragier,” corroborating the identity of his known wife Sarah Cragier, who died 4 March 1849 and was buried at Niskayuna.

**Absence from federal census 1850 — upper bound**

The 1850 United States Federal Census was the first to enumerate all household members by full name. A systematic search of FamilySearch collection 1488411 for John Witbeck and variants in New York (486 total candidates, top 50 retrieved and machine-ranked against MGRB-VP2) found no record matching John Perry Witbeck (born 10 March 1775, Schenectady County).² The closest candidate — “John W Witbeck,” born 1773, attached to a different FamilySearch tree person — differs in middle initial and birth year and is conclusively a different individual. Absence from a record whose enumerators were legally obligated to list every living household member is strong negative evidence that John Perry Witbeck had died before the June 1850 enumeration date.

**Absence from NY State Census 1855 — independent corroboration**

A systematic search of the New York State Census 1855, FamilySearch collection 1937366 (25 results for Witbeck/Whitbeck in New York, machine-ranked), found no individual consistent with the subject.³ The oldest candidates are born circa 1797–1805 — all 20–30 years too young. This independently confirms that John Perry Witbeck did not survive to 1855, reinforcing the conclusion that his death preceded the June 1850 federal census.

**Absence of direct death record — documented negative**

Systematic searches of FamilySearch “New York, Deaths and Burials, 1795–1952” (col. 1680846, 77,505 records) and “New York, Church and Civil Deaths, 1797–1963” (col. 2373798, 253,898 records) found no death or burial record for John Perry Witbeck or spelling variants (log_006, log_007). No cemetery abstract was found in FamilySearch “New York, Cemetery Abstracts, 1800–1965” (col. 2552111, 3 results, all definitively different persons) (log_009). This absence is expected and explicable: New York State did not require civil registration of deaths until 1880 (loc_001); since John Perry Witbeck died before 1850, no civil death certificate would have been created for him, and church burial registers for this era are incompletely indexed on FamilySearch.

### Analysis

Three independent evidential strands converge on the same bounded conclusion:

1. **The 1850 federal census** (primary information, negative evidence): John Perry Witbeck is absent from an enumeration that should have captured him at age ~75 if living.
2. **The 1855 NY state census** (primary information, negative evidence): independently corroborates death before 1855.
3. **The 1803 church record** (primary information, direct evidence): establishes he was alive in January 1803 — the last documentary trace.

The evidence is convergent but rests on absence rather than a direct death record. GPS research was not fully exhaustive: browse-only NY probate records (col. 1920234) were not imaged, and FindAGrave was not searched; either could potentially yield a burial date. These limitations prevent a “proved” tier.

### Conclusion

**Probable: John Perry Witbeck died before June 1850.** His last documentary trace is January 1803 (Gertrude Witbeck’s christening). The 1850 and 1855 census absences bracket his death to before June 1850. No exact death date is recoverable from available indexed sources; no death certificate exists, as NY civil registration began in 1880. The bounded conclusion — “died before 1 June 1850” — is the strongest statement the evidence supports.

# Mentor review: proof-critique on ps_002

## What you've done well
Your identity work on a_013/pe_017 is clean - the three-element name match plus the phonetic wife-surname corroboration (Krigier/Cragier) gives real confidence that this 1803 baptism entry belongs to your subject, and you documented the FamilySearch match score to back it up. Too many researchers gloss over what they didn't check - you didn't.

## What to address before moving on
Here's the thing that would most change how I read this proof: your bracket runs straight from 'alive January 1803' to 'absent from the 1850 census' - a 47-year silence - but the plan never checked the 1830 or 1840 federal censuses, both of which are indexed by head-of-household name and would have been a straightforward, cheap way to either tighten that bracket or add another convergent negative data point. Right now the 'died before 1850' conclusion is doing more work than the evidence chain fully supports.

Second, and related: your 1850 and 1855 census searches queried surname 'Witbeck' only. At roughly age 75 in 1850, it's entirely plausible John Perry Witbeck was living in a married daughter's or son-in-law's household - in which case a surname-only search for 'Witbeck' would never find him, dead or alive. That doesn't mean your conclusion is wrong, but it does mean the census absences aren't quite the clean, comprehensive negative you're presenting them as until you've also checked known children's households.

The negative census evidence is really the load-bearing evidence in this proof, but it lives only in the log entries and narrative prose - there's no assertion for it, so supporting_assertion_ids is just [a_013]. I understand this is a schema constraint (assertions need a record_id, and a nil search has none), but if there's any way to represent a negative-evidence assertion, it would make the proof's core claim structurally auditable rather than resting entirely on narrative description.

Running the 1830 and 1840 census searches (nil results still count and strengthen the case), plus a FAN-based recheck of 1850/1855 using the households of known children like Gertrude Witbeck, would let me treat the 'died before June 1850' bracket as genuinely reasonably exhaustive rather than resting on two census years searched under one surname.
